title_en: The Account of the Departure to the Divine Abode
translation:
THE ACCOUNT OF THE DEPARTURE TO THE DIVINE ABODE

The Dream That Occurred in Bhilapur (Original Samagam, page 308)

That account belongs to Dhanora and Puniyad. After that, in the year Samvat 1738, on the second day of the bright half of Magsar, at the temple of the devotees Bhagwandas and Bai Dhanbai in Bhilapur, a dream came — and this is what it was: devotee Jivandasji had lain down to rest. When just four ghadis of the first watch of the night had passed, all the old devotees who had already departed came there together and began to say, "Your saints are waiting a great deal for you there." Then Bhagwandas asked, "What are you thinking about?" Devotee Jivandasji said, "The whole company of devotees is going toward the western land, so I too must go along with them. The old devotees are waiting; that is why I must go westward. The period I fixed for the devotees was six months; this dream-encounter will be fulfilled in Puniyad."

THE ACCOUNT OF THE DEPARTURE TO THE DIVINE ABODE

That dream-encounter, to be fulfilled in Puniyad — here is what happened. What we call the "Samagam" is a text written in six sections, running from page 3 to page 313. In it:

Section 1 — pages 3 to 64: couplets (sakhis) of Kabir. Section 2 — pages 64 to 70: dohas of Jivanji; pages 70 to 102: couplets of Jivanji. Section 3 — pages 103 to 110: couplets of Jivanji; pages 111 to 147: hymns (kirtans) of Adhyaruji; pages 148 to 214: couplets of Kabir. Section 4 — pages 215 to 231: the Bhaktamal of Nabha Swami. Section 5 — pages 232 to 276: the account (Samagam) of Jivanji. Section 6 — pages 277 to 313: the account (Samagam) of Jivanji.

In this original Samagam, page 309 is torn, and pages 310 through 312 are missing altogether. The second side of page 312, and the reverse side of page 313, are where the writing begins again — but because the pages are torn, the text remains incomplete. For this reason, what stands in the latter part of the Samagam cannot be read. So devotee Nana Parekh combined the account of Jivanji Maharaj's departure to the divine abode with the text of the Samagam, and in this way presents, in heartfelt words, a vivid, lifelike picture of the Sadguru's final departure. Let us now offer an explanatory account of this record of the departure to the divine abode that he has written.

|| Sakhi ||
_Kabir guru videhi roop hai, jara maran nahi kaal,_
_jine guru jaana vansataa, taaka kaun haval ||_
(Das Kabirji says: the guru's form is one that has become free of the body, so for him there is no bondage to the limit of old age or death. But those who think of the guru as something that perishes — what a wretched state will befall them!)

_Gaai gavaavo jivanaa, kaahi sunaavo aap,_
_chidi chun jyoon det hai, aise sadguru baap ||_
(Nana Gopaldasji says: just as birds place morsels of grain into their chicks' beaks, so too is Sadguru Jivandasji a supreme father — he himself sings devotional hymns and performs bhakti, and also has his disciples sing devotional hymns, teaching them and making them hear the glory of devotion to God.)

Kundali:
_Gaai gavraave jivanaa, kahi samjhaave aap,_
_chidi chun jyoon det hai, aiso sadguru baap,_
_aiso sadguru baap, sevakni raksha karataa,_
_bataavi parmaarath panth, doreene aagal dharataa,_
_Trikam sadguru gun amaap, te samje koi harijan,_
_kahi samjhaave aap, gaai gavraave jivanaa._
(Nana Gopaldas says: the Sadguru himself sings devotional hymns and has us sing them, and explains to us the glory of devotional worship. Just as birds feed grain to their young, so he too feeds us the grain that is devotional worship. Such a Sadguru is a supreme father. Such a father-like Sadguru cares for his disciples; he shows them the true path and, taking hold of the rein, leads us forward on the path of devotion to God. Trikam says the Sadguru is filled with virtues beyond measure, which only some devotees come to understand — that the Sadguru instructs and explains, and sings and has others sing, devotional hymns.)

|| Ram Is Truth ||
The holy abode of Puniyad is the dwelling place of all the saints; there devotee Jivandasji resides. The chanting of Hari's kirtan, most auspicious, takes place there; the devotees have gathered together, and wherever this happens, supreme happiness arises. Love grows greater day by day; faith and dispassion (vairagya) come. [The devotees said:] "You are the Lord of grace; you have come to draw out (liberate) our souls."

|| Sakhi ||
_Kabir ke pade pragate, jagmaan Jivandas,_
_dhajaa baandhi dharma dadhaaviyo, jam kinkar paame traas ||1||_
(After Sadguru Kabir, Jivandasji appeared in this world. He proclaimed and spread the kirtan of the Namdev faith, sounded the drum of victory, and made it so firm that it could never be shaken — so that the messengers of Death became terrified.)

|| Doha of Devotee Jivandasji ||
_Kaanto haath Kabirke, tahaan sakal dharma toliyo,_
_jap tap tirath daan, taa moole meetho choliyo ||2||_
(Devotee Jivandasji Maharaj says: the scale of dharma, which shows no partiality of any kind, is held in the impartial hands of Kabirji. When, on that scale, every kind of spiritual practice was weighed, it was found that this path is supreme above all other practices, such as japa, austerity, pilgrimage, and charity.)

This (teaching of Namdev-Kabir means that) every other religion is mere husk and chaff — worthless rubbish. (Great Dharma Panchratnamala, first edition, page 316.) This statement does not appear in the second, third, and fourth editions. But the purpose of saying that other religions are mere husk and chaff is this: sanatan dharma — the Vedic religion, following the Vedic tradition that has continued since ancient times, with its practices of japa, tapa, yajna, vows, and pilgrimage — is negligible in comparison with the loving devotion of Namdev and Kabir. Thus this religion of loving devotion belonging to Namdev and Kabir is a religion that existed even before the Vedic religion, before all others; it stands at the highest, supreme level.

Trikamdas Gordhandas has written in a notebook called Chomika:
_Trilok brahmaand ekvisamaan, bhakt sam dharma na koy,_
_sant sajjan sahu kahe, samjethi sukh hoy ||16||_
(Trikamdas says: in the three worlds and the twenty-one universes — that is, in the entire cosmos — there is no religion that can equal or compare with the religion of the great devotees Namdev and Kabir. All the saints and good people say this. So if we understand and follow the way of these great devotees, our welfare will result.)

"This religion is the original, eternal (sanatan) one; having examined the three worlds and the twenty-one universes, no religion comes close to equalling this religion."

As to how sanatan dharma can be called mere husk and chaff — in a handwritten manuscript, on page 228, there was a thinker named Trikam who, criticizing sanatan dharma, said:

_Trikam taagaa bhramkaa, galme daaryaa sootaa,_
_nem prem pan nahi, kaljugke bhootaa ||58||_
(Trikamlal says: Brahmins wear the sacred thread of illusion around their necks, but they hold no discipline of any kind of devotion within them — so in this age of Kaliyug they are as troublesome as wretched, wandering ghosts.)

_Trikam do chelaa kiyaa, bhali kari bakshish,_
_sab janjaal chhodaayke, diyaa tokraa sees ||59||_
(Trikamlal says: such Brahmins made two or four followers, saddled them with a false burden of worship-obligations, and, having made them give up every other entanglement, loaded the basket of ritualism upon the disciple's head.)

_Sees tokraa dekar, sakal bhitaayaa bhram,_
_patharkaa choonaa karo, ehi sanaatan dharma ||60||_
(Trikamlal says: by loading the burden of ritualism onto the one who commissions the rites, they wiped away the misapprehension that harm would come from not following the path of ritual works. Thus, just as stones are fired in a kiln to make lime, so this sanatan dharma — the path of Vedic ritualism — burns living souls, like stones, in the three kinds of torment, and turns them to lime, so to speak: that is, it condemns souls to the wretched grind of repeated birth and death.)

The newspaper Gujarat Samachar, dated 6 March 2003, page 5, writes in its "Dharmalok" column: rebellion and struggle for reforming the sanatan dharma system can be seen. Abroad, there was Martin Luther; in this country, saints such as Kabir, Kutch's Dada Mekan, and other wise, gifted figures of their time indeed expressed the most intense outrage against the prevailing system, did they not?

|| The Dream-Vision of Bhilapur ||
In the year Samvat 1737, on the second day of the bright half of Magsar, at the temple of devotees Bhagwandas and Dhanbai in Bhila[pur], devotee Jivandasji had lain down to rest. When four ghadis of the night had passed, a dream came, and this is what appeared in it: the old devotees who had already departed, the whole company, had gone there and were waiting for him. All the saints were gathered together, and there a discourse and kirtan were taking place. When one watch of the latter part of the night remained, two devotees came there; they appeared before devotee Jivandasji in vision — no one else could see them. He heard them conversing. They were a great abundance of radiant beauty; they held a red staff in hand; their bodies were fair; they were in the fullness of youth; they had no beard or moustache.

Two devotees came bearing a red staff. Why was the staff red? Red is usually taken as a colour signifying danger. But red is also the colour of love. And the colour of peace and happiness is white — that is why, on auspicious occasions, red roses and white abir (fragrant powder) are scattered. Redness signifies the joy and delight of deep love; thus Das Kabir has spoken of "redness" in this way. Those who came to meet Jivanji Maharaj were lovers of this kind.

_Laali mere laalki, jitaa dekhoon titaa laal,_
_us laali dekhan main gayi, tab main bhai (bhi ho gayi) laal gulaab ||17||_
(Das Kabirji says: the loving devotee became so absorbed in love of God that when he went to experience the joy of that divine love, he found that wherever he looked, he experienced nothing but that very love. And as he went to witness that experience, he himself became so absorbed in divine love that he himself turned into the very embodiment of that loving experience.)

Those devotees spoke to Jivandasji: "I have come to summon you — there Kabirji is present, Rankaji is present, Namdevji is present, Senaji is present, Dhanaji is present, Pipaji is present, Rohidasji is present; Bhagoji too is there."

Devotee Jivandasji asked in particular, "Is Kabirji there?" Then that devotee said, "Ramdevji too is there. Countless devotees are waiting for you — how can things proceed there without you? That is why the devotees have been waiting a very long time." — "Yes, Kabirji is there," [came the answer], and devotee Jivandasji felt great joy.

One can see how great the love Jivanji Maharaj held for Das Kabir must have been, that even where countless devotees already were, he still made sure to confirm whether Kabir was there. He asked: even if all the devotees are there, is Kabir there as well? And on learning that Kabirji indeed was there, he became very happy.

Jivandasji said to those devotees, "Here the devotee(s) and Gopal have great hope; I shall come in the sixth month."

Jivanji's devotees held such deep affection for Jivanji Maharaj that they wished he would stay with them a long time and grant them the benefit of loving devotion. So one can see how much feeling Jivanji Maharaj himself must have held for his devotees, that even to the messengers of God he made the promise that he would come after six months. Thus, even though Jivanji was entirely free of worldly desire, one can see how much affection he held for his devotees.

The devotee(s) said to devotee Jivandasji, "Without you nothing proceeds; we have been waiting a very long time."

Just as Jivanji expressed such love for Kabirji, it becomes clear that Kabirji and the other devotees held just as much love for Jivanji — that they too suffered the pain of separation without him. Jnaniji Maharaj has written a hymn describing what such separation feels like among those who love in this way.

|| Raag Maru ||
_Sant sandesho laayo, sun virahani man laay sundari,_
_Hari preetam tum maahi vase, sakal kahe samjhaay sundari ||tek||_
_Jahaan too jue tahaan sundari, bhitar bharam nivaar sundari,_
_man hi mahi man mohanaa, dekho samje vichaar sundari ||1||_
_Saansaa sakal nivaarke, antargat mein Hari jue sundari,_
_nishche hoy ke nirakhle, poogah mile he soe sundari ||2||_
_Hilmil aanand upajaa, poori mankee aash sajni,_
_dukh koi vyaape nahi re, avichal sadaa vilaas sundari ||3||_
_Tab virahini sukh paaiye, saambhaal piuka sandesh sujni,_
_gyani aatmaa aanagiyo, paayo updesh sundari ||4||_
(Gyaniji Maharaj says: a messenger has brought a message from the saints — listen, O grieving bride, bring it to your heart, O beautiful one. Your Beloved dwells within you — all say so, to make you understand, O beautiful one. Wherever you look, O beautiful one, banish the illusion within you. Within your very mind is your Enchanter — see this, and think it over well, O beautiful one. Having cleared away all doubts, see Hari within your inner self, O beautiful one; once you gain certainty and behold Him directly, you will find yourself united with Him, O beautiful one. Mingling together, joy is born, and the heart's longing is fulfilled, O companion; no sorrow shall trouble you again — there is everlasting, unchanging bliss, O beautiful one. Then does the separated bride find happiness, heeding her Beloved's message, O companion. Gyani says the soul was made joyful, having received this teaching, O beautiful one.)

Devotee Jivandasji said, "My Bal Gopal has a wish for Janmashtami; I shall come after performing the Janmashtami festival. Bow down to those devotees and give them my Ram-Kabir greeting. Also tell them that I have the Janmashtami festival first." Then Bhagwandas asked, "What are you thinking about?" Jivandasji said, "The whole company has departed, going toward the western land; the old devotees are waiting, so I am going westward. That dream-encounter will take place in Puniyad. Also tell them I have the Janmashtami festival [to keep] first." Then those devotees withdrew. Here the devotees asked, "Maharaj, with whom did you hold this conversation? We saw no one."

Devotee Jivandasji said, "The devotees who came, from wherever that place is, came to summon me; they pressed the invitation very affectionately, and I made a promise of six months." That dream-encounter that was to be fulfilled in Puniyad — here is what happened: in Puniyad, at Shyamdasji's temple pavilion, where he had lain down to rest, devotee Jivandasji too had lain down to rest. In the year Samvat 1738, on the second day of the bright half of Jeth, a devotee came like this: with tilak and tulsi, wearing bright clothing; his body was fair; there was no trace of beard or moustache at all; he was in the fullness of youth; there was an abundance of radiance about him; he held a red staff in hand. He spoke, saying they were summoning him.

On the second day of the bright half of Jeth, Samvat 1737, the day the six-month promise came due, the devotee(s) came to summon him. Then Jivandasji said, "I have a wish for the festival; I shall come after performing the Janmashtami festival. Tell those devotees my Ram-Kabir greeting. Also tell them that the Janmashtami festival is two months and twenty-one days away. My Bal Gopal has a great longing for it; the Lord of grace will fulfil his wish. That is why they called me, having set the time-limit of the festival." Then, since Shyamdas and Narandas were near him, he related the whole encounter to them in full.

The devotees asked, "What conversation took place?" Then Jivandasji said, "Devotees had come to summon me; there the devotees are waiting a great deal, so now I must go. I have made the promise regarding Janmashtami first." So he sent for Kahandasji, and when twenty days remained of the appointed period, he had all the devotees summoned; everyone came and sat together. The kirtan of Hari continued day and night from the full-moon day of the bright half of Shravan, without a break.

Jivandasji said, "Prepare the provisions and ingredients [for the feast]; prepare the leaf-plates; hasten the festival preparations; prepare the food — khaja, jalebi, and curry, these three dishes." All the devotees set about their duties. [He said,] "Summon all my Bal Gopals — without me, who will fulfil their wishes?" Then the day of the eighth (Janmashtami) arrived, and everyone came and sat together.

Devotee Jivandasji spoke:
|| Sakhi ||
_Sadguru sandesaa moklaa, kachambchaan sab aav,_
_naam chintaamani jivanaa, je bhaave so paav ||3||_
(Nana Gopaldasji says: the Sadguru has sent an invitation for everyone — young and old, great and small among the people — to come into the disposition of performing loving devotion, to join in bhakti to God. And by joining in it, in whatever way suits you, receive the precious jewel that is the divine Name, which fulfils your heart's desire; become absorbed in that divine Name and take joy and delight in it.)

Kundali:
_Sadguru sandeso mokle, kachaanbchaan sab aav,_
_santaa vachan vichaarine, akho parampad paav,_
_akho param pad paav, kahe chhe Jivandaadaa,_
_samjhaavi chhe vaat, saabad shikhaaman saadaa,_
_Trikam kahevaa bhaav, samje nahi jan achhalkaa,_
_kachaanbchaan sa aav, sadguru sandesaa moklaa._
(The Sadguru has sent such a message: come, everyone, together with your children, and join the fellowship of devotees, to join in devotion to God. Understanding the words spoken by the saint in this way, may you attain refuge in the imperishable divine Name; may you attain that exalted abode — so says the honoured elder Jivandada. Trikamdas feels the wish to explain the secret of his words, but thoughtless people, unaware of what is imperishable, do not understand that the Sadguru has extended this invitation for everyone, together with their children, to join in devotional singing and worship.)

_Baal boodhku jivanaa, Ram bhajanki aash,_
_shoorveer bhaagi chale, daante pakadi dhaas ||4||_
(Jivandasji Maharaj says: from children to the elderly, all devotees hold the yearning to perform devotion to God; they possess great firmness and steadfast resolve. As for the rest — those who used to display valour on the strength of ritualism, the Vedic path, the scriptures, the Puranas, and the paths of yoga and knowledge — they, having lost their courage, came, helplessly, to take refuge in the divine Name.)

Devotee Jivandasji said, "Brothers, if anyone tries to deceive you, do not be deceived by it. The true God is Morli Manohar, the charming flute-player, alone; were there any other, then Brahma and the Vedas would lead you astray."

Morli Manohar alone is the true God — that is, whatever deities exist apart from him would separate us from Morli Manohar, that is, from the true divine essence. Because the divine essence that is Morli Manohar is God's original, true form. From that very essence, and from the navel of Sheshshayi Bhagwan, a lotus arose; from that lotus Brahma came into being, and through Brahma the threefold-natured creation was brought forth. Therefore Brahma and the Vedas, being derived from the quality-transcending divine essence, separate us from devotion to Hari and load our heads with obligation. Brahma became separated from God, and the Vedas became separated from Brahma; thus Brahma and the Vedas, having become separated from God, establish their own authority and carry on their own grandeur.

For five days the joyful festival continued, and all the devotees flourished. Four devotees remained to render service; their names were: 1. the devotee Laldasji; 2. the devotee Gopaldasji; 3. the devotee, third, of Nadiad (Goriyada), Haridasji; 4. the fourth devotee, Rupa Bhagat.

The day of Jivandasji's appointed time arrived. The devotees came and sat together. Devotee Jivandasji asked, "Has everyone — all the Bal Gopals — come?" Kahandasji said, "Maharaj, your Bal Gopals — everyone has come and is seated in the pavilion." Devotee Jivandasji said, "Set my seat there in the pavilion; let me have sight of the devotees." Then Jivandasji went and took his seat. All the devotees came and fell at his feet, sensing that this was the final occasion; they made many entreaties: "Maharaj, take care of us."

Devotee Jivandasji said, "Namdev-Kabir will care for you and protect you." Devotee Jivandasji further said, "We entrust the service to Kahandasji; go and circumambulate the devotees — that will bring [their] grace." Kahandasji went round in circumambulation, bowed to Jivandasji, had his own neck-garland placed [on him], applied the tilak, and all the devotees paid their respects.

Then the devotees said, "Show your grace to Shyamdasji; he is of your own household." Devotee Jivandasji had given his garland to Kahandasji and entrusted the service to him, but he had not given it to his own son. Thus this great soul showed no self-interest of his own. And when the assembly of devotees said that Shyamdasji was indeed of his own household, he took hold of Kahandasji's hand and, through Kahandasji's hand, had the garland placed upon Shyamdasji.

Devotee Jivandasji said, "Dharma belongs to naad (sound)." Devotee Jivandasji took Kahandas's hand, had the garland moved with the thumb, applied the tilak with the thumb, and the garland was placed on Shyamdasji; all the devotees paid homage.

There are certain terms that support the threefold-natured maya (illusion), and even though they turn one away from the path of devotion, they present themselves as if depicting devotion to God — and by such allurement they can lead astray those without a true guru. But if one has found a true Sadguru, one will not be taken in by such enticing words. Among such misleading terms are: japa, tapa, pilgrimage, vows, ritual observances, spirituality, self-knowledge, yoga, meditation, yajna, and supernatural powers. Among these, the words "Omkar" and "Naadbrahm" too have such an effect that they throw devotees who are weak, soft, and incomplete in understanding into confusion. Such confusion has arisen in devotee Nana Parekh and others, who, in this account of the departure to the divine abode, tried to present the statement "dharma belongs to naad." So let us briefly consider the confusion that exists regarding naad and bindu (the drop, or point).

The reason we write here that dharma belongs to naad is this: for devotion to God, one must follow only whatever command the guru has given. Only through such guru-oriented followers can the tradition of loving devotion continue. Here, though the garland was given to Kahandasji, it was given on to Shyamdasji through Kahandasji, at the devotees' request — meaning that the path of loving devotion is the same for every lover of God. This is the intent behind the words "dharma belongs to naad." As for the term "Naadbrahm," that word denotes "Omkar," and therefore, for those of us who follow the loving devotion of the threefold nature marked by the double-r sound, dharma — that is, bhakti — cannot rightly be called a matter of naad in that sense. Jivanji held an open, selfless attitude toward all devotees equally; he did not, therefore, show favouritism toward Shyamdasji out of attachment. The magazine Kalyan, year 35, issue 7, page 1043, writes that the soul becomes conscious through the voice of the inner self; any sound other than that is maya.

"This very naad is that ignorance or illusion which, by its own influence, produces in the soul the illusory reaction of individuated existence. In truth, naad and the individual soul — or maya and the individual soul — are one and the same."

The devotees of Surat district have published a book titled Ramkabir Bhakt Bhajan Sangrah. Its second edition has been given the title "Naad Brahm." A devotee from there told me, "I am the one who had this name given." I did not object to it, but the name "Naad Brahm" seems attractive, and so one is tempted by it; but they probably do not know that the meaning of "Naadbrahm" is "Omkar," and our devotees do not know that there is a difference between Omkar and the double-r sound of this tradition. Neither Omkar nor Naadbrahm can express the true sentiment of the word "bhajan."

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj would never use the word "Naadbrahm." Omkar has been called a "respectable-looking thief," and it is by being deceived by this respectable thief that some of our devotees, mistaking dharma for a matter of naad, have gone astray. Trikamdas Gordhandas, who fought in the trust case, referring to the phrase "dharma belongs to naad," wrote a poem (kavit):

_Naad gharam sadguru kahyo, swaamipane santaap,_
_sadguru vachan uthaaptaan, guru drohnoon paap,_
_guru drohnoon paap, kadaapi tale na kothi,_
_sant shastra sahu gaay, juo uthlaavi pothi,_
_Trikam taalne shaap, vans vaaras sheed saahi rahyo,_
_swaamipane santaap, naad gharam sadguru kahyo._
(Trikamdas says: the Sadguru has said that dharma belongs to naad; and holding pride in lordship [over the seat] leads to suffering the bondage of worldly existence and karma. By transgressing this teaching the Sadguru gave, one incurs the sin of wronging the guru. The sin of offence against the guru cannot be averted by anyone — so the saints and scriptures say; search through the books and read for yourself. Trikamdas says: [Jagdishbhai,] stop bringing upon yourself the curse of the sin of wronging the guru. Why are you clinging to the claim of hereditary succession to Jivanji's seat? You will suffer from the pride of lordship, for the Sadguru has said that dharma belongs to naad.)

This poem was written in connection with the trust case; when it says to give up lordship, it was written to urge that the whole temple be handed over to the trust. It was not Jivanji who said that dharma belongs to naad — the devotees said this out of misunderstanding. As heir to Jivanji, it is not the seat, but the property and the temple, that he was asked to hand over to the trust.

Kahandasji asked, "What do you say, Maharaj?" Devotee Jivandasji spoke:
|| Sakhi ||
_Kahnaa thaa so kah liyaa, ab kahaa kahu samjhaay,_
_sant sevaa karo jivanaa, je Raghupati hoy sahaay ||5||_
(Jivandasji Maharaj said: whatever essential, ultimate truth there was, I have already told you. What more should I now explain? But serve the saints, so that Ram will become your helper — Ram's grace will come upon you.)

Trikamdas Gordhandas has written, in his diary of [Samvat] 2025, on page 43, Kundali no. 3:
_Kahenaa thaa so kah diyaa, ab kahaa karu samjhaay,_
_sant sevaa karo jivanaa, Raghupati hoy sahaay,_
_Raghupati hoy sahaay, sant dhar sadaa rakhchaa,_
_Dropadi soni kaaj, dharyo chhe roop rasaalu,_
_Garud taji gaj kaaj, sukh shayyaane taj diyaa,_
_ab kahaa karu samjhaay, kahenaa thaa so kah diyaa._
(Jivandasji Maharaj said: whatever ultimate, supreme truth there was, I have already told you by now. What more, beyond that, should I explain? But you must serve the saints, and then God will help you; God will give you assistance, for he always watches over and protects the abodes of the saints. He took on a beautiful form to protect the honour of Draupadi and of Seni Bhagat; and for the sake of the elephant, he abandoned Garuda, and even left his serpent-bed, and ran at once to help. Now what more is there to say, to explain further? Whatever was worth telling, I have told it all.)

In the Chomika notebook, page 174, Kundali no. 161 is written:
|| Kundali ||
_Kahenaa thaa so kah diyaa, ab kahaa karu samjaay,_
_sant sevaa karo Jivanaa, Raghupati hoy sahaay,_
_Raghupati hoy sahaay, santne sharane jaataan,_
_tale trividh taap, ikoter paavan thaataan,_
_Trikam harakh naa maay, sadguru gnaane samajiyaa,_
_ab kahaa kahu samjaay, kahenaa thaa so kah diyaa._ Jivandasji Maharaj says: I have already told you the essential, ultimate truth; so what more should I explain now? But serve the saints, so that Ram will become your helper. By taking refuge in the saints, Ram will show you grace; moreover your threefold sufferings will also be removed, and even your seventy-one generations will be made pure. Trikamdas says: those who understood according to the Sadguru's teaching felt great joy; so now what more should I say — whatever supreme truth was worth telling, I have already told it.

He spoke further: in Radhikaji's hand is the water at the centre; the other incarnations are its waves, and the waves break. He comes taking form in many guises, but the guise itself passes away — it is the play that is real: the great Supreme Lord who grazed the cows in Gokul, He is the real one.

|| Sakhi from His Own Mouth ||
_Gokulmen vaaso vasu | surate kaaj saraad |_
_apni soje Jivanaa | brij taji anat na jaau ||6||_

Jivandasji Maharaj says: I dwell abiding in Gokul, and by my attention I carry on the working of creation; but of my own wish I do not go anywhere, leaving Braj.

When Bhagwan Shrinathji departed from Govardhan, he took two vows.
_Brij taj anyatra na jaai ho | yah mere hai tek |_
_Bhootal bhaar utaar ho | dharo roop anek ||1||_
Bhagwan says: I shall not go anywhere else, leaving Braj — this is my pledge; to relieve the earth of the burden of unrighteousness, I shall take on many forms.

_Brijvaasi Vallabh sadaa | mere jeevanpraan ||_
_tinahe nek na bisar ho | mohe Nandbaabaaki aan ||2||_
(Jagdish's notebook no. 199, page 33.)
Bhagwan says: those who dwell in Braj are always dear to me as my own life; I shall not forget them even for a moment, and if I do, I swear it by Nand Baba. — Bhagwan's seven [daily] darshans take place at Nathdwara, and the eighth, the resting (shayan), takes place in Braj; that same resting-place is at Jatipura. The extent of Govardhan is six miles, and its circumambulation is fourteen miles.

|| The Word of Baba Kabirji || Vasant ||
_Dekho Shri Vrindavanmen sadaa aanand | jahaan dharan gagan nahi chand ||tek||_
_Raadhaa Maadhav ek naam | ek hi roop aur ek hi gaam |_
_meri surat pahunchi nij dhaam | sadguru mile mohi saare kaam ||Shri||2||_
_Roop aroop Hari kaho na jaay | roop aroop gopi raas maanhe |_
_mohe mangal chaar diye bataay | urdh baahu gahi bhari laaye ||Shri||3||_
_Asht kamal aath ghaat | jogi jangam lahe na baat |_
_trigun rahit Hari gun niraat, soi hridaa kamal beech aayo ||ghaat||Shri||4||_
_Aad ant Kaalindi teer | Shri Vrindavanki meethi seer |_
_sadguru vachane gharjo dheer | nij gun daave Daas Kabir ||Shri||5||_

Das Kabirji says: Look, look indeed — in this Shri Vrindavan there is always joy alone to be found, in that place where there is not even earth, sky, or moon. There, only the one Name of Radha and Krishna exists; their form, too, is one and the same, and their place too is one and the same. My attention has reached that personal abode of God. I found a Sadguru, and so this work of mine was accomplished. What form Bhagwan holds, or whether he is without form, cannot be told; that Bhagwan, with form or without it, is there with the gopis in the circle of the raas dance. I have shown the four beneficent gifts — tilak, tulsi, the company of saints, and the Name of Hari — as blessings; raising their hands high, they brought divine grace in abundance. Even though yogis strive by way of the eight petal-landings of the eightfold lotus — the stations from the muladhara to the brahmarandhra in hatha-yoga — by which one is meant to cross over worldly existence, they do not find the way across. Bhagwan is the one alone who is beyond the three qualities, wholly pure in every attribute; that Bhagwan has come to the inner landing-place of my own heart-lotus. Such is that Bhagwan: from beginning to end, on the bank of the river Jamuna, there flows the sweet stream that is the loving devotion of Shri Vrindavan.

(On this "sweet stream": the revered Yadunathji writes, in Litiyu no. 26, on the reverse of page 4 1/2: "The shingi fish lives in the salty ocean, yet it drinks sweet water. A fish that wishes to drink sweet water should not give up the company of the shingi fish — only then can it drink sweet water, only then can a fish come to drink sweet water.") Das Kabirji says: hold fast, with full faith, to this teaching that the Sadguru has given.

Vaishnav Jivandasji said: this rasa is unbroken — it is not broken even for the space of a single wink.

|| The Word of Mehtaji || Raag Sindhudo ||
_Ji re akhil Vrindavan akhil brij sundari | akhil avanish avar raasdhaari ||_
_akhil leelaa ras rahe swar raman range rame | akhand Mathuraa te trilokthi nyaari ||tek||_
_Ji re hans saaras rame mor markat tahaan | akhil madhup kokilaa tahaan bole keer |_
_sheet mand sugandh sameer sheetal vahe | akhil Kaalindeenun subhag neer ||1||_
_Ji re akhil gopi gop gwaal gauvaachharun | akhil morali madhuri dhoon gaaje ||_
_Raadhikaa Raadhikaa ratan akhil kare | nij mantra nij naam nij dharam saaje ||2||_
_Ji re surat jyaare sanchare Shesh sukhaasane | Aadya Naaraayan naam dhaare ||_
_Vaikunthvaasi Vaikunth saayak sadaa | raas mahali kshanu nav sidhaare ||3||_
_Ji re Brahmaa Shankar Sati Sanakaadik aadi yati | pavan swapne praveshnaa tahaan ja thaaye ||_
_nigam ne aagam Shesh anudin rate | akhil Narsaiyo te raas maanhe ||4||_

Narsinh Mehta says: in the whole of Vrindavan, all the beauties of Braj, together with the Lord of the whole universe who holds the raas dance, sport at will, out of love, in the unbroken play of the raas, in the bowers of delight. That whole Mathura is unlike anything in the three worlds. There, swans and cranes sport, and monkeys too are there; there, bees, koels, and parrots are forever calling. A cool, gentle, fragrant breeze blows there with its coolness; the lovely waters of the Jamuna flow on continually. All the gopis, cowherds, cows, and calves are there; the sweet sound of the flute continually resounds. There, everyone continually repeats only the name "Radhika, Radhika." Each one takes up their own mantra, name, or code of conduct in devotion to that Radhika. When the yearning is drawn toward that Bhagwan who reclines upon the comfortable couch of Shesha, he then bears the name Aadinarayan. That Bhagwan, who forever dwells in Vaikunth and gives aid to Vaikunth, never departs from the raas even for a moment. Even Brahma, Shankar, Parvati, and ascetics such as Sanak and his brothers cannot enter into it even in dream, nor can the wind. The Vedas and the scriptures of dharma, and Sheshnag himself, forever repeat and remember His name; and in that very raas, Narsinh Mehta abides forever.
